question: The same coffee from the same chain costs more at the gate than in town. Why?
answer: Because the buyers can't leave. Behind security there is no café across the street, so the airport lets its few spots to the highest bidder and takes a cut of every sale. Where an airport forbids the mark-up, it goes: Portland, Oregon, has required 'street pricing' since 1988.
move: When a price looks unfair, ask who can't walk away.
ask: Where am I paying more simply because I can't easily go elsewhere?

start.text: Same coffee, same chain: dearer at the gate.

levels.text: The café hands the airport a cut of every sale, on top of rent.
Airports live off shops and parking almost as much as off flights.
A café can pay that cut because its buyers have nowhere else to go.
Security turns the terminal into a closed town: no next street.

options: Beans cost more to fly in

source: ACI World, Airport Economics Report; Port of Portland concessions policy
reference: Airports Council International, Airport Economics Report (non-aeronautical revenue about 40% of airport income); Port of Portland, PDX street pricing policy, in place since 1988

question: Your ears pop as the plane climbs, even though the cabin is pressurised. Why isn't it kept at ground level?
answer: To spare the metal. Holding ground-level air at cruise would push on the hull about 40% harder, flight after flight, and metal tires with every stretch: in 1954 two Comet jets broke apart from fatigue cracks. So rules allow a cabin as thin as air at 2,400 metres.
move: A design that seems stingy is often paying for something you can't see.
ask: What hidden cost is that annoying limit paying for?

start.text: Your ears pop as the plane climbs.

levels.text: The cabin air thins as you climb; the air behind your eardrum lags.
The cabin is only kept as dense as the air on a mountain.
Ground-level air inside would push on the hull 40% harder, every flight.
Metal tires each time it is stretched. Less push, longer life.

options: Full pressure would tire the hull

source: FAA, 14 CFR §25.841; UK Ministry of Transport, Comet inquiry report (1955)
reference: 14 CFR §25.841 Pressurized cabins (cabin pressure altitude not more than 8,000 ft); Report of the Court of Inquiry into the accidents to Comet G-ALYP and G-ALYY, HMSO 1955

question: Bread goes stale even sealed in its bag. If it isn't drying out, what is happening?
answer: Its starch is turning back into crystals. Baking melts the starch into a soft, disordered gel; as the loaf cools, the long molecules slowly line up again and stiffen the crumb. Cold speeds this up and heat undoes it, so a stale roll revives in a hot oven. Freeze bread; don't chill it.
move: Stale isn't dry; it's starch going back into order.
ask: Which 'obvious' cause have I never actually checked?

start.text: Bread goes stale even sealed in its bag.

levels.text: Stale isn't dry: sealed bread keeps nearly all its water.
The crumb stiffens instead, and heat makes it soft again.
Cold makes it worse: bread stales faster in the fridge.
Baked starch is a soft jumble; cooled, it packs into crystals.

source: Gray & BeMiller, Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety (2003); McGee, On Food and Cooking
reference: Gray, J.A. & BeMiller, J.N. (2003) Bread staling: molecular basis and control, Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety 2(1): 1–21; Harold McGee, On Food and Cooking (2004)
